steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Psychologists report that children in nine-month schools typically forget a significant amount of schooling during summer breaks.

steps.label: Conclusion (We should conclude)
steps.body: The twelve-month schedule is to be preferred insofar as academic learning is concerned.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: [The twelve-month schedule with three month-long breaks] will insure that students will not forget their schooling during their breaks.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Line up what the psychologists studied against what the author concludes.

The research is about one schedule. Children in nine-month schools forget a significant amount during summer breaks. That's it. Nothing in the evidence is about the twelve-month schedule. Yet the author claims that schedule "will insure" students do not forget during their breaks.

Where does that guarantee come from? The author is assuming forgetting is a problem of the nine-month schedule only. But the twelve-month schedule still has breaks. Three of them, each a month long.

Given that kids forget over a long summer, how could we argue the twelve-month plan is no better? Maybe kids forget plenty in a month, too. If a month away wipes out most of what a summer away does, the twelve-month schedule could mean three rounds of forgetting instead of one.

So the gap is in the comparison. The evidence shows a bad result in one situation, says nothing about the other, and the author treats the other as free of it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument assumes, without evidence, that forgetting during breaks happens only under the nine-month schedule. A "fails to consider" version would also work: the argument fails to consider that students might forget during month-long breaks too. Either way, the answer should point at the missing evidence about the twelve-month schedule.

notes.body: The argument never weighs academic against nonacademic learning. It limits itself on purpose: the twelve-month schedule is preferred "insofar as academic learning is concerned." Test the presumption: if academic and nonacademic experiences were worth exactly the same, would the argument lose anything? No. It needs no view about their comparative worth.

The two groups here, children on a nine-month schedule and children on a twelve-month schedule, differ in exactly the way the argument cares about: how the breaks are arranged. That distinction is the subject of the argument, not an arbitrary line. The problem is what the author assumes about one side, not where the line is drawn.

This matches the prediction in formal words. The "two situations" are the two schedules. The "undesirable result" is forgetting schooling over a break. The evidence ties that result to the nine-month schedule, and the author takes for granted that it belongs to that schedule alone, so the month-long breaks are assumed to be safe.

When a comparison has evidence about only one option, check whether the argument quietly assumes the other option is free of the problem. That unstated "only" is what an answer like this one names.

Questioning the sample attacks the one part of the argument that has evidence behind it. The research only needs to describe children in nine-month schools, and nothing suggests it doesn't. Grant that the data is perfectly representative and the argument still fails, because no one has shown that month-long breaks avoid the same forgetting.

The author accepts the psychologists' finding and uses it as the main evidence. That view is never rejected later in the argument. If anything, the argument leans on the research too far, by stretching a finding about summer breaks into a promise about month-long breaks.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes; the Evaluate and Goal chased overall-learning side effects instead of the real gap (no evidence that month-long breaks avoid forgetting), and notes were padded.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Making vagrancy illegal means transforming many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Vagrancy laws increase crime while purporting to reduce it.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Watch the word "crime" change jobs between the evidence and the conclusion.

The evidence is about classification. Vagrancy laws turn "innocuous everyday occurrences" into crimes. Acts that were legal yesterday are illegal today.

The conclusion is about amount. Vagrancy laws "increase crime." The columnist sets this against the laws' purpose of reducing "criminal activity," which makes it sound like people are now doing more harmful things.

Picture a park where twenty people nap on benches every week. A vagrancy law passes. The same twenty people nap on the same benches. On paper, the town now has twenty crimes a week that it didn't have before. Has anyone's behavior changed? No. The count went up because the label changed.

So the evidence supports only "more acts are now called crimes." The conclusion needs "people are committing more crime." The columnist slides from one claim to the other as if they were the same.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument confuses relabeling acts as crimes with an actual increase in criminal activity. It might say the argument fails to distinguish the two, or that it uses "crime" in two different senses.

notes.body: The columnist calls these occurrences "innocuous," which means harmless. The whole complaint is that harmless acts get treated as crimes. So the argument presumes the opposite of this answer: it treats the occurrences as not harmful.

The columnist never says vagrancy laws produce more innocuous occurrences. The occurrences stay the same; only their legal status changes. This answer invents an increase in the occurrences and then criticizes a causal inference the argument never makes.

Ask whether naming the occurrences would fix anything. Suppose the columnist listed them: napping on a bench, standing on a corner. The argument would still slide from "more acts count as crimes" to "more criminal activity." The vagueness isn't what breaks the argument.

On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken. Suppose crime would rise even without vagrancy laws. That says nothing about whether the laws themselves add to the count, which is the columnist's claim. Other causes of crime leave the argument untouched.

This names the slide we predicted. "An increase in criminal activity" is what the conclusion claims. "The reclassification of certain occurrences as crimes" is all the evidence shows.

When a conclusion reuses a word from the evidence, check whether the word means the same thing in both places. If it doesn't, the right answer says the argument fails to distinguish the two meanings, just as this one does.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes, a Goal that named the task more than the answer, and thin wrong-answer notes without a test.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The best seafood gumbo requires fresh okra.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: If this claim were true [Chris's okra supplier cannot reliably supply fresh okra], then Chris's customers could not count on getting good seafood gumbo.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence is a conditional. Fresh okra is required for the best seafood gumbo:

best gumbo → fresh okra

Its contrapositive tells us what happens without fresh okra:

no fresh okra → no best gumbo

That's what the evidence supports. Now read the conclusion closely. Without reliable fresh okra, customers could not count on good gumbo:

no fresh okra → no good gumbo

"Best" became "good." Those are different standards. A gumbo can be good without being the best. Without fresh okra, Chris might still serve a very good gumbo that just isn't the best one possible.

So the critic takes a requirement for the top level of quality and treats it as a requirement for a merely good level. Given the evidence, how could we argue customers can still count on good gumbo? Say good gumbo doesn't need fresh okra at all.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument assumes that whatever the best seafood gumbo requires, good seafood gumbo also requires. It might also say the argument fails to consider that good gumbo could be made without fresh okra.

notes.body: The critic never relies on the competitor being right. The argument only says what would follow "If this claim were true." A biased source can still make a claim, and a hypothetical about that claim stands or falls on its own logic. The bias never touches the reasoning.

This describes a quality passing from an ingredient to the dish: stale okra, so stale gumbo. The critic does something different. The okra lacks freshness, and the critic concludes the gumbo lacks goodness. Those are two different qualities, so this isn't the error. The real error is the shift from "best" to "good."

This is the tempting one, because it uses necessary and sufficient language and mentions both "best" and "good." Check what the argument does with fresh okra. It treats fresh okra as required for good gumbo: no fresh okra, no good gumbo. That's treating it as necessary, not sufficient.

To confuse it with a sufficient condition, the critic would have to argue that fresh okra guarantees good gumbo. The critic never says that. The error is a necessary condition moved from one standard to another, not a necessary condition flipped into a sufficient one.

This matches the prediction. The evidence says fresh okra is necessary for the best seafood gumbo. The conclusion uses fresh okra as if it were necessary for good seafood gumbo.

When a conclusion leans on a requirement from the evidence, check that the requirement is attached to the same thing. Here it moved from "best" to "good," and that move is the flaw this answer describes.

The critic's hypothetical already allows for this. A supplier who "cannot reliably supply" fresh okra may still deliver it on some days, and customers still couldn't count on getting it. Considering the possibility changes nothing, and it never touches the jump from "best" to "good."

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes, no Goal step, diagrams packed inline, and the tempting C trap got a thin note.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: People can either fight for anarchy or they can tolerate totalitarian government control. History shows that government control of all facets of human life destroys the spirit, making life miserable. Anarchy allows each individual the freedom to pursue a personal course of happiness.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: People should fight for anarchy.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the first sentence, because the whole argument rests on it: people "can either fight for anarchy or they can tolerate totalitarian government control."

Those are the two extremes. Anarchy means no government at all. Totalitarian control means government controls "all facets of human life." What about everything in between? A government that runs the courts and the roads but leaves your personal life alone is neither one.

Now look at the support. The evidence attacks only total control: it destroys the spirit and makes life miserable. Fine. Given that, how could we still argue against fighting for anarchy? Point to a third option. If limited government is available, rejecting totalitarian control doesn't push us to anarchy. It could just as easily push us to the middle.

The argument works only if those two options are the only ones. That's a false choice: two options presented as if nothing else exists.

Notice the flaw sits in a premise. We usually accept premises as true, but when an argument reaches its conclusion by knocking out one side of an either/or, the right answer can point out that the either/or was never complete.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument treats anarchy and totalitarian control as the only two options, or that it fails to consider some form of government between the two.

notes.body: The argument does give a reason anarchy beats total control. Total control "destroys the spirit," while anarchy "allows each individual the freedom to pursue a personal course of happiness." So the claim that the argument makes no attempt to explain this is false. The answer misdescribes the argument.

The argument names tolerating totalitarian control as an option and then recommends against it. Naming an option is not endorsing it. Nowhere does the anarchist say people should tolerate totalitarian government, so there is no contradiction.

This reverses the direction. The evidence is that totalitarian control makes life miserable, and the conclusion is that people should fight for anarchy. Check any "infers X from Y" answer: Y must match the evidence and X the conclusion. Here they are swapped.

The anarchist says "history shows" that total control destroys the spirit. That is an indication of evidence, even if the details aren't given. This answer says there is no indication at all, which the text contradicts.

This is the false choice. The first sentence offers only two paths, and the argument needs that to be true: rejecting one path proves the other only when nothing else is available.

When an argument gets to its conclusion by eliminating one option, check whether it has shown the options were the only ones. If it hasn't, an answer like this one names the flaw.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes, no Goal step, a padded Evaluate, and wrong-answer notes without a test.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Many of the words used to describe web sites evoke ideas that are usually associated with real estate. The common law of trespass usually applies to cases of encroachment on real estate.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It is reasonable to extend that law [trespass] to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence is about words. We call a web page a "site," and we talk about "visiting" it. Those words also describe land.

The conclusion is about law. Trespass law, which protects land, should be extended to protect property in cyberspace.

The bridge between them is an analogy: web sites resemble real estate, so they should be treated like real estate. But what resemblance has been shown? Only that we use some of the same words. That's a similarity in vocabulary, not in anything that matters to the law.

Test it with another shared word. We "drive" traffic to a web page. Should traffic laws apply to web pages? Of course not. Shared vocabulary doesn't show that two things are alike in the ways a law cares about, such as how they can be entered, damaged, or used without permission.

Given the evidence, how could we argue against the conclusion? Point out that a web site might share nothing with land except the words we use for it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the analogy between web sites and real estate rests only on shared words. A "fails to show" version works too: the argument fails to show the two are alike in any way that matters for trespass law.

notes.body: The argument never claims that people consider cyberspace property to be real estate. It claims only that some words for web sites "evoke ideas" of real estate. And even if many people did consider it real estate, that would be one more fact about how we talk and think, not a reason the law should treat the two alike.

Circular reasoning needs a premise that already assumes the conclusion. Check the premises: some words for web sites evoke real estate, and trespass law usually applies to real estate. Neither says trespass law should cover cyberspace. The conclusion goes beyond them, which is the opposite of circular.

The tempting part is the first sentence: most lawyers think copyright law is the best protection for web site owners. But that isn't evidence against extending trespass law. Copyright law could be the best tool while trespass law is still a reasonable addition. The evidence gives weak support for the conclusion, not support for the opposite.

This matches the prediction. The "similarities that constitute the analogy" are the shared words "site" and "visiting," and "merely verbal" names exactly what's wrong with them.

When an argument concludes that two things should be treated alike, ask what similarity it has actually shown, and whether that similarity matters for the treatment it recommends. Here the only similarity is in vocabulary.

The argument mentions expert opinion only to move away from it. Most lawyers favor copyright law, and the argument ends up recommending trespass law. It never defends its view by pointing to what experts believe.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes, no Goal step, an Evaluate built on a first-person aside, and thin wrong-answer notes.

steps.label: Conclusion (This indicates that)
steps.body: Swahili culture was to some extent influenced by Oromo culture.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In the 14th and 15th centuries, the Swahilis built tombs with big pillars and paneled outsides. Those types of tombs are also super common among the Oromo, who were in contact with Swahili. But no other culture known to have mixed with the Swahili has these types of tombs.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the curious fact. The Swahili and the Oromo both built tombs with large pillars and paneled facades, and no other people in contact with the Swahili built them.

The historian's explanation: Oromo culture influenced Swahili culture. That's a claim about direction. The style traveled from the Oromo to the Swahili.

What evidence points that way? None. The evidence shows the two cultures share the style. It dates the Swahili tombs to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, but gives no date at all for the Oromo ones.

Given that, how could we argue the Swahili were not influenced by the Oromo? Flip the arrow. Maybe the Swahili built these tombs first and the Oromo picked up the style from them. Everything in the evidence fits that story just as well. (The two cultures could even have arrived at the style independently.)

For the Oromo to have influenced the Swahili, the Oromo must have had the style first. The historian takes that for granted.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the historian assumes the Oromo built these tombs before the Swahili did. A "fails to consider" version works too: the argument fails to consider that the Swahili may have influenced the Oromo.

notes.body: The historian's point is about a building style: large pillars and paneled facades. Suppose the Oromo used these structures for something other than tombs. The style could still have passed from one culture to the other. What the buildings were used for doesn't touch the question of who influenced whom.

This flaw needs a timeline: A came before B, so A caused B. The historian gives no such timeline. There's a date for the Swahili tombs and nothing for the Oromo ones. The real trouble runs the other way: the argument needs the Oromo to come first and never shows it.

Drawing a narrower conclusion than your evidence allows is caution, not a flaw. And the premises don't strongly support anything broader than influence "to some extent." The trouble is the direction of the influence, not its size.

This sounds like the classic alternative-explanation answer, so test it. "Takes for granted" means ask whether the argument needs it. Suppose a third civilization did create the first such tombs, passed the style to the Oromo, and the Oromo passed it to the Swahili. The conclusion still holds: Swahili culture was influenced by Oromo culture. The argument doesn't need to rule out a third civilization, so it doesn't assume one away.

This is the prediction. Influence runs in a direction, and the conclusion picks one: Oromo to Swahili. That requires the Oromo to have built these tombs first, and the historian offers nothing about when the Oromo built them.

Whenever a conclusion says one group influenced another, ask what establishes the order. If nothing does, the assumption that the source came first is the gap.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes, wrong-answer notes around 100 words that repeat the same point, and the D trap never ran the necessity test.

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: There are celestial objects in this galaxy that generate light but are not stars.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Stars generate light. Planets do not generate light. There are many other celestial objects in this galaxy that are not planets.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Sort the celestial objects in this galaxy into three groups. Stars generate light. Planets don't; they only reflect it. And there are "many other celestial objects" that are neither.

The conclusion says some of those other objects generate light. Why? The evidence never says whether the other objects generate light. The author seems to reason: planets don't generate light, these objects aren't planets, so some of them do. Here is the shape:

planet → does not generate light
some objects are not planets
so, some of those objects generate light

That's an illegal negation. The rule tells us what is true of something that is a planet. It tells us nothing about things that aren't planets. The argument works only if planets are the only objects that don't generate light.

Given the evidence, how could we argue the conclusion is false? Suppose every one of those other objects is dark, like a planet. Then there are many objects that are neither stars nor planets, and none of them generates light.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The stem says "fails to consider," so look for a possibility that would wreck the conclusion. The best one: objects other than planets might also fail to generate light. The answer might put it exactly that way: planets are not the only objects that do not generate light.

notes.body: Run the "fails to consider" test: would this weaken? Suppose planets are the only objects that reflect light. Then the other objects don't reflect light. That still says nothing about whether they generate it; they could do neither. The gap about generating light stays exactly where it was.

The argument is only about this galaxy. Whether this galaxy holds a tiny share of the universe's objects or most of them, the question is the same: do any of its non-star, non-planet objects generate light? The size of the galaxy's share doesn't touch that.

Objects in other galaxies are outside the argument. The conclusion is about light-generating objects "in this galaxy." Knowing that some objects elsewhere generate light can't make the conclusion any more or less likely to be true here.

The argument never says light is the only difference between stars and planets. It uses light because that's what the conclusion is about. Stars and planets could differ in a hundred ways and the gap would remain: nothing shows the other objects generate light.

This names the overlooked possibility. The argument works only if planets are the only objects that don't generate light, because then anything that isn't a planet would have to generate it. Say other objects also fail to generate light, and the many non-planet objects no longer prove anything.

On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. This one removes the only route to the conclusion.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes, an Evaluate that mocks the argument and uses gendered pronouns, a rambling Goal, and wrong-answer notes over 100 words each.

steps.label: Conclusion (therefore)
steps.body: The choice between seeing a specialist or a general practitioner for needed PT will not affect one's chances of major improvement.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Among patients who received less than six weeks of PT, about 31% showed major improvement, whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist. Among patients who received PT for longer, about 50% showed major improvement, again regardless of whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion is about one patient's choice: picking a specialist or a general practitioner won't change your odds of major improvement. The evidence is about whole groups: across all patients, the two kinds of practitioner get the same rates.

Can equal group rates hide real differences? Try numbers. Suppose there are two kinds of injury, sprains and fractures, and each practitioner sees as many of one as the other. General practitioners get major improvement in 50% of sprains and 12% of fractures. Specialists get 12% of sprains and 50% of fractures. Both average 31%. The records look identical.

Now you have a fracture. Does your choice matter? Very much: 50% with a specialist, 12% with a general practitioner. The equal totals hid the fact that each practitioner is better at a different injury.

So given the evidence, how could we argue the choice does matter? Point out that the overall numbers could be an average of very different results for different injuries.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument overlooks that the two kinds of practitioner might do better with different kinds of injuries or patients. Then equal overall rates would not mean equal odds for any one patient.

notes.body: The argument never mentions "any improvement." Its evidence and its conclusion are both about major improvement. So it can't be inferring something about major improvement from facts about any improvement. This answer criticizes a step the argument never takes.

The argument doesn't need to know which injuries need short treatment and which need long. It compares the two kinds of practitioner within each length of treatment, and the rates match in both. Knowing why one injury takes six weeks and another takes longer would not reveal any difference between the practitioners.

The evidence is records of whether patients "showed major improvement," not patients' opinions of their practitioners. A patient could feel more warmly about a specialist and still show the same improvement. Bias in how patients feel about practitioners doesn't touch the outcome records the argument relies on.

Percentages already account for group size. If 31% of 100 general-practitioner patients and 31% of 1,000 specialist patients improved, the rates are still equal. Unequal numbers of patients would not, by themselves, make the matching percentages misleading.

This is the hidden-subgroup problem from the numbers above. Equal overall rates can come from each kind of practitioner excelling at a different injury, and then the choice matters a lot for any one patient. On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken: here it does, because it shows equal averages can sit on top of real differences.

Whenever an argument moves from equal group results to "the choice won't matter for you," check whether the group could split into parts where the results differ.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes, an Evaluate and Goal that chased the word 'necessary' instead of the hidden-subgroup gap, a typo in the Evidence, and a correct-answer note that misdescribed E with an outside 'harder cases' story.
